column2: **Undo/redo as recorded transitions.** Every mutating operation runs through a `tracked()` wrapper that snapshots HEAD before/after. Undo applies the inverse (soft reset for commits, ref restore for branch deletion, …) and validates the repository hasn't moved since — corrupting-the-repo is structurally prevented, and hard-reset-style undos refuse to run over uncommitted work.

- [x] AI: provider-agnostic (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Ollama, LM Studio) plus installed AI CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Antigravity) — commit messages, diff/conflict explanations, PR descriptions, staged-change review with team conventions (global + per-repo `.angkorgit/review.md`), background execution with stop, full-size reading views

**Live updates via a debounced watcher.** A `notify`-based filesystem watcher (400 ms debounce, `.git` noise filtered down to HEAD/refs/index movements) emits a single `repo-changed` event; the frontend refreshes status — or everything, when HEAD moved externally. Editing in an IDE or committing from a terminal reflects in the UI within half a second.

**Graph layout in the domain layer.** Lane assignment (`GraphLayout`) is pure TypeScript, incremental, and unit-tested. Feeding page N+1 never changes rows from page N, which keeps the virtualized list stable while history streams in. Rendering is a per-row SVG slice — O(visible rows), regardless of repository size.

**Tauri v2 + libgit2 (git2-rs).** A native Rust engine gives sub-millisecond status/diff operations and avoids shelling out to `git` for hot paths. `vendored-libgit2` keeps builds hermetic across macOS/Windows/Linux. Every command runs on a blocking thread (`spawn_blocking`) so the UI thread never waits on I/O.

column2: **Conflict resolution as data.** Conflicted files are parsed into text/conflict blocks (`parseConflicts`), the resolver mutates block resolutions, and `serializeResolution` writes the result. Unresolved blocks re-emit their markers, so a half-finished session never destroys data.

Faster to open, lighter, and narrower on purpose. GitKraken took the workflow ideas further than anyone and I learned from it, but I wanted the twenty-five features that matter rather than the hundred. Fork is closer in spirit, though it is not open source and not on Linux.

The build isn't signed with an Apple developer certificate yet, so Gatekeeper asks once. Right-click and Open, or install through Homebrew, which clears the flag for you. After that the updater handles new versions and verifies each one with a signature.

**Verified destructive operations.** Discard (file or all) re-checks status afterwards and reports what could *not* be discarded, so cases libgit2 silently skips (submodule pointer changes) surface as actionable messages instead of silent no-ops.
